speechtext: I think the hon. member is right.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thank you. I was pointing out in what way those of us in this section of the chamber differ from the other political parties in this house. All of us are anxious, I take it, to solve the great social and economic problems confronting our people, but all the other political parties are trying to solve these matters within the limits of the capitalist system, that is, without interfering with the property relationships which exist within
the present capitalist structure of society. We take the position that the difficulties and trials we are meeting to-day are due to the workings of that system and not to maladministration by government, to bad business, or to lack of business ability on the part of individuals, and we hold that those troubles cannot possibly be solved under the present system. Therein lies the essential difference between other parties and ourselves, and I think modern history is with us, because it goes to show that those governments which have made any progress towards solving their social and economic problems in the past few years are those which have taken steps to control the economic life of their respective nations. So then, we say, the only solution for the world to-day, the only way to end unemployment, to get rid of our debt, to bring prosperity and to establish peace is for the countries of the world to adopt socialism as their economic system. I am quite sure that this does not seem so fantastic to-day as it did a few years ago. As I go round, talking with people in all walks of life, I find that, whatever they may say in public, they have no hope that they are going to solve their problems under the present capitalist system. They will say that socialism is bound to come but it will not be just yet. I am reminded of a statement supposed to have been made by Herbert Hoover, ex-President of the United States. He is reported as having said:
When I contemplate capitalism I see a precipice leading either to communism or fascism.
He sees a precipice where the drop will be either to communism or to fascism. It is not necessary to fall into either of these states, providing we do the right thing in time, but if we allow the conditions that exist to-day to get worse, something will happen and we may not be able to control the situation. What may develop then no one can say. But in all countries where democracies exist it is within the power of the people to go easily and surely into a new social order where production will be carried on to supply human needs and not for the making of profits. Under our present system the attempt to find markets in which to dispose of surplus goods, leads inevitably to war.
I have taken three different countries which have made some progress in dealing with their social economy during the depression years. The first one, Great Britain, was mentioned the other day by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), who remarked, I think, that Canada had followed Great Britain in almost
The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis

all things with the exception of balancing our budget. Canada has not followed Great Britain at all. There were certainly some lame and hesitating attempts made to follow Great Britain during the last parliament. I am not suggesting for one moment that Great Britain has accepted socialism, but she is providing a certain amount of social control over the economic life of the country. I have taken excerpts from an article which appeared in Current History of November, 1935, and I would like to read some of them:
To the older generation, familiar with the British slogan of "No food taxes" and the doctrine that only through cheap food for the working man could there be low wages, low costs and a competitive advantage in world markets for British manufacturers, it is almost incredible that to-day about one-third of British agricultural produce is under priceraising marketing schemes, implemented in nearly every case by highly effective protection against foreign trade. The first to be thus dealt with was wheat-it is strange to remember that it was for free wheat that the battle of the corn laws was fought and won in the hungry forties. Instead of a marketing scheme, wheat was given a subsidy or "quota" in 1932. A levy was imposed on every sack of flour imported into Great Britain or milled within the country. The proceeds went to the British wheat grower to make up the difference between the price he actually received and the standard price of about $1.40 a bushel.
And yet we wonder why British imports of wheat from Canada are not so great as they were some years ago. Then the next paragraph:
The acquiescence of the greater part of the people in a program that involves taxation and increased costs of living for 93 per cent of the population in behalf of the 7 per cent who derive their income from agriculture indicates that rugged individualism as an ideal is fast vanishing from the British mind.
There is very much more of this that is worth reading, but I shall content myself with one more excerpt from the article, and I should like to draw the attention of the government to the necessity of doing something along these lines in the Dominion of Canada, because after it is done we shall have an asset to show, and it will bring comfort to many of our people. I quote again:
The most effective subsidy and possibly the greatest influence in the government's whole recovery program, is the aid that has made possible the immense housing program how being carried out in Great Britain. Since the armistice there have been built in Great Britain about 2,700,000 houses, almost one-half of which have been subsidized by the government or by the localities. Under the present government, the program has been speeded up. During the four years ended on March 31, 1935, about one million houses were built in England and Wales. In its last

session parliament passed a housing bill under which within five years all officially condemned slums will be demolished and sufficient houses provided to do away with overcrowding. At the most this program is expected to cost the public treasuries only $50,000,000 a year-not a staggering sum, the proponents of house construction as a recovery measure like to point out, in comparison with the money spent upon battleships, heavy guns and bombing planes.
Then it goes on:
The worst criticism is that it cannot last forever, and the slump may be bad. To this the government replies that it can see good results for at least five years ahead, after which, come what may, the British masses will be decently housed.
So, if the slump comes after the government have taken the first step in the organization and control of the economic and social life of the people, they will be better prepared to take the next step, if that slump should come before they have embarked upon a fully socialist program in that country.
During the last year we have heard a great deal about Sweden. So much that to-day Sweden has become a competitor with Russia for the tourist traffic, for the people who are anxious to see what has been accomplished in the last few years. I have under my hand an article which appeared in the La Fleche Press of February 20, 1936, and reprinted in the Saskatchewan Liberal of February 27, 1936, so I suppose there will be no objection if I read it in this house. The article states:
The cooperative societies of Sweden own and operate ten per cent of all industry and handle some 50 per cent of all retail trade in such essentials as food, clothing and shoes, says Stuart Chase in Government in Business, and continues as follows:
"They broke one private monopoly after another by threatening to organize their own supply. This has proved far more effective than anti-trust laws. The price of lamps was driven down from thirty-seven cents to twenty.
"Sweden has obviously mastered the yardstick technique with which Mr. Roosevelt is now struggling. She has the highest standard of living in Europe, higher even than for the mass of Americans. She is now about fifty per cent collectivized-including the cooperatives as public business. Private business has resigned itself to the inevitable, and from time to time actively cooperates in some aspect of state enterprise."
In addition Sweden has maintained the democratic principle in government and in industry, so that if we do not wish to follow other more drastic examples certainly we should not be afraid to follow the example which has been set by Sweden.
Now I wish to mention another country, which during the last sixteen or seventeen years has received a great deal of attention, some favourable and some not quite so favourable. It has this outstanding distinction,

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
however, that it is, I think, the only country in the world which has made continuous economic and social progress through all these years of depression.	I refer now to the
soviet union, and I am going to quote an authority to whom I do not think the house will object. The individual who wrote the article is, I believe, above reproach, and I think the periodical in which the article appeared will be quite acceptable to hon. members. The article is by Sir Frederick Banting, KJ3.E., and it appeared in Canadian Business, the official organ of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, of February, 1936. May I say, for the benefit of those who do not know-though I do not suppose any hon. member needs to be told-that Sir Frederick Banting is one of the discoverers of insulin and is in receipt of an honorarium, I think it is called, from this government amounting to some $7,500 yearly for his services to the people of Canada and of the world. My hon. friend from Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) says that Sir Frederick Banting receives something from the Ontario government as well. He writes:
The greatest experiment that the world has ever known, has just been carried out within the Soviet Union ...
Note this:
In the successful carrying out of this experiment, science was a major factor. Science and the fruit of science had been almost denied these people from the beginning of their history, until 1917. The Bolsheviks suffered privation, fought and if necessary died for those far-sighted leaders who promised the people education and science.
Then he goes on:
In order to understand the situation in the Soviet Union to-day it is necessary to realize that before the revolution only about ten people out of every one hundred could read and write.... The vast majority of the people were backward, down-trodden peasants who lived on farms or in small villages. Of the 170,000 doctors (at the rate of one doctor per one thousand population) -
That is the number they should have had.
-there were but 19,000 and these were, for the most part, located in the cities of the west and in the army and navy.... During the past ten years progress has been stupendous.
Then he goes on to indicate the progress that has been made in education, medical science, scientific research, production, and so on. I shall content myself with reading the last paragraph in the article:
All of these huge enterprises-
Referring to the industrial life of the country:
-require men of executive capacity, intelligence, foresight and judgment. These qualities are to be found in the men who rise to office
within the Soviet Union. The life and activities of their great commercial and industrial men do not greatly differ from the life and activities of industrial men in our country- nor does the financial man, banker and organizer of industry, differ so much from those that perform this service in other countries. There are privileges and luxuries that our financial leaders buy. In the Soviet Union these privileges and luxuries are given to him by the people. They honour service. Honour, appreciation and trust of comrades spur and inspire men to plan and work for the common good of all.
We are told in this country that unless there is the incentive of profit people will not do anything. Could anything be moTe false? We are told that in Russia people in every walk of life are continuously working for the common good without any thought of profit or private gain. But all the industries of Canada have the profit incentive. Here the means of production are used by their owners not to provide goods and services for the needs of the people but as a means of levying tribute on the people. Dr. Banting goes on to say:
There is no unemployment in the Soviet Union. Conditions are improving very rapidly. Everyone is tremendously enthusiastic. The health of all is cared for by the state. All people have the opportunity to rise as high as their talents and industry will permit in whatever field of endeavour they may select. Every person's future is invested in the state. The state in turn provides for the education of children and an old age pension. This sense of security brings happiness and peace of mind and permits true culture.
Can we say that in this country? Is there a sense of security here, even among those who are in employment, even among those who are in business, even among those who are fairly well off? No; there is no sense of security to-day for anybody. He continues:
The soviet government is building a gigantic structure on the solid rock of science and research. For this reason there now remains not a vestige of doubt as to the future success of the Soviet Union. Her future is doubly secure because no people in the world so fully realize that the science of to-day is the research of yesterday, and the research of to-day is the science of to-morrow.
When you compare that with what we have been attempting to do in this house during the last three months-unplanned activity when there was any activity at all; a dribble here, a dribble there; no coordination and no connection-it is no wonder that people are almost in despair.
I have another item here from Doctor Banting. Speaking in Hamilton, Ontario, on November 27, 1935, he said:
You rarely see a case of tuberculosis that requires hed treatment in Russia. Trade union
The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis

doctors examine the workers before they enter factories and they are placed under care immediately if any signs of disease are detected.
But in this great rich country whenever anything of the kind is mentioned we are always met with the question: Where can we find the money?
There came into my hands to-day a copy of the Monthly Review of Lloyd's Bank Limited for April, 1936, a rather conservative publication, I assume. In it I find a leading article by R. J. Truptil entitled The Economic Evolution of Soviet Russia, 1917-1936. It says:
It must be remembered that although the peace of Brest-Litovsk was signed in 1918, the Bolsheviks had to fight for several years, until 1921, against insurrections and interventions on many fronts.
And we helped in the fight against them. Even now we have not the trade relations with Soviet Russia that most other nations of the world have. After giving a very complete summary of the situation and the increase in production, he ends the article with this statement:
The economic revolution achieved in the Soviet Union is without parallel. In fifteen years-for it_ is fair to reckon only from the end of the civil war-one of the poorest and most backward nations has achieved simultaneously an industrial equipment and a complete transformation of its agricultural methods. Through many changes of policy, the Bolsheviks have gradually extended social ownership to all the means of production, transport and trade.
Yet they are keeping up their enthusiasm. They are working, they do not expect the state to keep them; they are themselves the state.
Their system is socialist. Although individual property can be acquired in the form of savings, state bonds, a house, a car, or a few animals, and although such property can even be inherited up to an amount of 50,000 roubles, there can be no individual ownership of the means of production.
That is, they are not allowing anyone to exploit the people for private gain.
_ As the system develops we may see issues of industrial debentures, but it seems reasonably certain that shares will not reappear.
Furthermore, it is not possible in the U.S.S.R. to live on unearned income....
Evidently they are finding no difficulty with the A plus B theorem either. They are finding it quite easy to increase the welfare of their people as production increase, and they are not issuing social dividends or social credit. All the production of the country belongs to the people, and until the production of this country belongs to the people I do not care how much the money system is

manipulated, you are not- going to get anywhere. Then the article concludes:
As it is, the system works,-
That is the final proof of any system.
-and this in a country of 170 million inhabitants, which for size, diversity and natural wealth can be compared only with the United States. The Soviet Union is thus becoming a leading factor in the world and it would be a profound mistake to ignore it.
In that connection let me say that to-day, because of the national control of its working class, Russia is the greatest factor for peace in the world. In fact so far as there is any guarantee of peace it comes from Russia and from the working class in the other countries where they have any voice at all in the government of the country.
I will conclude, Mr. Speaker. I had no intention of speaking so long. But I hope the house will realize that we cannot go backward, much as in my opinion the finance minister would want us to do. We are out of that stage just as surely as the chick that has left its shell, and we can never return to it, any more than the chick to the shell. So let us look to the golden age of the future, not to the golden age of the past-because there never was a golden age of the past.
On motion of Mr. Blais the debate was adjourned.
